lines: I have mended this same net four times. It is more mend than net at this point.
Everyone here goes to bed when it gets dark. There is nothing else to do, so, bed.
My father wakes me by standing in the doorway saying nothing. It works, which annoys me.
I am the one they send when something needs carrying a long way. That is my whole role.
There are eleven people here my age. Eleven. I know all of them far too well.
The traders came through and I asked one of them what it is like further along the coast.
He said: same, but further along. I have been thinking about that answer all week.
I can do every job here. That is not a boast, it is a complaint about the number of jobs.
The weather turns and everyone announces it, out loud, one after another, like it is news.
I fixed the pump myself and nobody has noticed, which I have decided is fine.
The old ones tell the same story three times a week and I have started mouthing along.
Somebody has to do the early tide. It is always me, because I am the one who complains least.
I have read every book here. Both of them. Several times.
There is a path out of here that I have walked to the end of, and then walked back.
The rule is you do not go past the ridge alone. I have gone past the ridge alone.
My mother says I am restless like her brother was. She does not say where her brother went.
I sharpen everything. Knives, hooks, the spade. It is the only job where I can be left alone.
The little ones follow me around. I pretend to hate it. It is roughly fifty-fifty.
I can tell what tomorrow will do from the way the birds sit tonight. I am usually right.
Nobody here has ever been more than three days' walk from this spot. I have checked.
The level comes up about a hand a year. You cannot see it happen. You can only see it having happened.
I have lived through one move already and I was too small to remember it, which feels like a waste.
There is a step at the bottom of the path that my mother says used to be halfway up.
You measure a place here by how many years it has left, and everyone does the sum quietly.
The maps are all wrong and nobody redraws them, because by the time you finish they are wrong again.
I know exactly which of these houses will go first. Everybody does. Nobody says it at dinner.
The salt gets into the wells before the water does. That is the actual warning, not the tide.
We say the level, or this year, or the tides. Nobody says the flood. I have started noticing that.
My grandmother's village is a shape under the water that you can only see from up high.
The old ones talk about a coastline that stayed still and I genuinely cannot picture it.
Every family here has a house their grandparents built that you would now need to swim to.
The frogs move uphill a year before the people do. Watch the frogs, my father says.
We are all descended from people who stopped running. That is not a compliment, exactly.
There are doors down there that still swing when the current goes past them.
The wet mark on the stone is higher than my father's mark and his is higher than his father's.
Nobody argues about whether it is rising. They argue about how long they have got.
I asked how long we have here. My uncle said: longer than me, shorter than you.
Our boat is named after a girl who drowned before I was born and we say the name like it is nothing.
The adults have a whole vocabulary for not saying the thing. I have learned it fluently.
There is a key on a nail by our door and the door it opens has been under water for years.
My aunt swims down and touches a door handle every year on the same day and then comes up and says nothing.
I know where every drowned house is because I have been made to learn it, like a poem.
The old ones cry at rain and blame the wind and everyone lets them have the wind.
There is a bowl in our house with a blue bird on it that came out of somebody else's kitchen.
We use it. That is either respect or it is just that we needed a bowl. Probably both.
My mother lists the families of the low street when she cannot sleep. I know the list now too.
Somebody cut two letters and a heart into a beam that is now underwater. Nobody knows whose.
The stairs down there still have their handrail. You can hold on all the way to the bottom.
There is a shelf in every house here that belongs to somebody dead and stays empty.
My grandfather saved a chair and lost a brother in the same week and only talks about the chair.
The names outlast the places by about two generations. Then they go too.
There is a garden fence under the water with the gate still shut. Somebody shut it on the way out.
We found a child's shoe in the shallows last spring. The whole beach went quiet at once.
Everybody's family used to be bigger. That is just a sentence people say here.
Seven things are still standing. Everything ordinary is under. People take that personally.
The pointy ones are called markers because people decided the water stops at the top of them.
That is not a fact. That is a thing people needed to be true, so now it is repeated as one.
The great wall is thought to be a dam that failed, and people walk its whole length looking for the break.
There is no break. I have said this out loud once and I will not be doing it again.
The ring of arches is supposed to have been a cistern. Children are told lions drank there.
The carved city was cut out of the rock, not built, so people argue it is older than the water.
The argument is really: did the world exist before this. Everyone pretends it is about masonry.
The calendar stone is meant to say when the water stops. It has been read a thousand ways.
The uplanders copy the mountain terraces and say build like that and you live. They copied it wrong.
The tomb is for one person and it is the most beautiful thing there is and nobody argues about it.
That is what gets me. Everything else is a fight and the tomb just gets agreed with.
Nobody knows who built any of it. Everybody speaks as if they do. Both of those are true at once.
My grandfather's version and my teacher's version cannot both be right and both are told with total confidence.
The wall-walkers are the ones who walk the great wall end to end. They pass through for salt.
They have been looking for the break for generations. They will keep looking. That is the point of them.
Somebody chalked a wonder's name on the mill wall as if that would hold the water off.
The wrong stories are load-bearing. Take one out and I do not know what people would do.
They are teaching everyone letters now. Everyone. Even the ones who will never write a word.
The reason is: somebody has to be able to read the books in fifty years. Nobody finishes the sentence.
I am being taught things by people who will not be here to see whether they were useful.
My mother copies a book by hand every winter so there will be two of it, then four.
I am the one who will have to move next. Everybody knows it. Nobody has said it to me.
They are cutting names into stone instead of writing them on paper now. That is a decision about time.
There is a shelf built in the cave, planed smooth, empty, sized for books that do not exist yet.
The seeds are in wax-sealed jars at the back of the cold chamber and they are not for us.
I asked who they are for. I got the longest silence I have ever got out of an adult.
Half the arguments here are about going higher and the other half are about staying.
The people who go up send word back saying come up. The people who stay do not send word.
My grandmother planted a row of trees that fruit in nine years. She has said she is fine about it.
Somebody will come through hungry, she said. That is the whole argument, and it is a good one.
I want to leave and I am also the only one here who can fix the pump. Those two facts are at war.
We are learning songs with the place names in them so the names last longer than the places.
Everyone my age is being trained as a replacement for somebody specific. I know who mine is.
The old ones apologise at the end. All of them, in the end. It is a horrible thing to watch.
I have decided I am going to see the tomb before I die. I have told nobody this.
Bail, mend, bail, sleep. I could do the whole day with my eyes shut and some days I nearly do.
The boards are worst when they have dried and then got wet again. That is when people go in.
I have gone in twice. Both times somebody laughed before they helped.
The rope goes furry where it sits at the waterline. Furry means replace it, not tighten it.
We eat fish. I would like it on record that I have opinions about how much fish we eat.
The tide table is nailed by the door and my father reads it aloud like a prayer.
There is a knack to the outside walkway in wind. Lean in, do not look down, do not hurry.
Everything here is tied to something else. If one thing goes, you find out what else was tied to it.
The houses stand on legs and the legs get longer every time somebody rebuilds them.
You can date a house here by counting the rungs somebody has added to its ladder.
Ours has eleven. The oldest one in the row has nineteen and it leans.
There used to be four rows out past us. Now there is us, then water, then more water.
At the big tides the sea comes over the boards and everybody lifts their feet and keeps talking.
Nobody out here says flood. We say the level. I only noticed that after somebody from uphill said it.
The uplanders call us stubborn. We call them cowards. Both sides mean it affectionately, mostly.
You can see roofs under us on a still day, which is a thing I stopped finding strange.
We are the last row and the last row is always somebody. It just used to be somebody else.
At the lowest tide of the year the schoolyard railing comes up out of the water like a row of teeth.
The little ones dare each other to touch it. I have touched it. It is a railing. That is all it is.
My mother was born in a room that is directly under where I sleep. She points down when she says it.
Anzu moors her raft to a chimney out there. It was her aunt's chimney, back when it had a house under it.
The old well is down there full of sea water, which everybody calls a joke and nobody laughs at.
We swim to the shrine ledge on her birthday and leave something and it washes off by morning.
We do it anyway. I used to think that was stupid. I have stopped thinking that.
My uncle can find any doorway under this village by feel, in the dark, eyes closed. He has proved it.
The bricks down there are older and a different colour and nobody makes that colour any more.
We live over drowned houses and argue about a carved city none of us will ever see.
Somebody chalked a line on the mill and called it a marker line, meaning the water stops there.
It stops nowhere. But the chalk made two families sleep better, so nobody rubbed it off.
The wall-walkers pass through for salt. Not one of them can swim. Not one, ever.
They walk a wall looking for a hole while we bail a house. Everybody has their thing.
The ring of arches held water in on purpose. We hold water out on purpose. Somebody should write that down.
The uplanders say build like the mountain terraces. You cannot terrace open water. I have said so.
Everyone here agrees the tomb is the most beautiful thing there is. Nobody here has seen it.
The markers are on dry land and we are out here on sticks. That comes up in arguments a lot.
Some families are going up in the spring and some are not, and the two halves have stopped eating together.
We teach the little ones to swim before they can properly walk. Nobody calls that what it is.
My mother says we bail until we cannot bail, and then we go, and not one season sooner.
They are cutting the names of the drowned houses into a roof beam so the beam carries them.
I am to know these walkways by heart, in the dark, in wind. That is not a chore, that is a plan.
My grandmother announced she will not move, in front of everybody, so now she cannot take it back.
The good rope goes on the ladder and everything else gets the bad rope. That is a new rule.
Somebody asked outright how long this row has left. The whole room found jobs to do.
I will be the one who closes this place up. I worked that out by myself and I have not told anyone.
Half these houses are empty and I know which three still have doors that properly shut.
The gulls take anything you set down for one second. I have tested this more than once.
There is a cart with no wheels behind the last house that has been mine for two years.
My job is turning the drying fish so they cure evenly. It is boring and I smell of it constantly.
There is a bell on a post for weather. It has been rung twice in my life and I missed both.
The sand gets in no matter what anybody does and people still shout about it every day.
A family left a whole set of pots behind when they moved and we simply started using them.
The beach glass is the only good thing here. The sea rubs it soft and then gives it back.
Boats tie up where carts used to turn round. There is a ring in the wall for each of those things.
Follow the road out of here far enough and it simply becomes sea. There is no end to it, it just stops mattering.
Every year one more family moves from the bottom row to the top row. Nobody has ever gone the other way.
You can tell how long a house has stood empty by how far the weeds have climbed the door.
There is a dark line on every wall here at the same height. That is where the water gets to now.
We had a garden. It went salty three summers ago. It is where the nets live now.
The old beach was twice this wide. There are people alive who walked on the part that is gone.
This place is halfway through leaving and has been halfway through leaving my entire life.
The house on the corner still has curtains and nobody has lived in it since I was small.
There is a boat in the weeds with a family name painted on it. That family is three villages up now.
My mother stands in the empty street sometimes and does nothing at all and then comes back in.
We took the door off my grandparents' house and it is our table. We eat off their door.
Somebody's height is scratched up a doorframe in the empty house, and then it stops, mid-childhood.
There is a doll in the window at number four and everybody has silently agreed to leave it there.
The bakery oven is still standing in the ruin. My father claims he can still smell it.
He cannot. But I am not going to be the one who says so.
A wall-walker came through last month, doing the whole length of the great wall, looking for the break.
His feet were in a state. He would not stop to rest properly. They never do.
The pointy markers are supposed to show where the water stops, which would mean somebody knew in advance.
Every roof beam in this village is cut to the mountain terrace angle. Supposedly. Nobody has checked.
Pilgrims go to the calendar stone and come back saying it did not say anything, and go again next year.
My uncle argues the carved city predates the water and therefore proves the world had a before.
He is right and he is completely unbearable about it, which are two separate problems.
Children here are told lions drank at the ring of arches. Nobody has ever seen a lion.
The tomb is the only one nobody argues about. That should tell us something and I cannot work out what.
Mid-decision, my mother calls it. She has called it that for four years running.
They are pulling the good beams out of the empty houses before the sea gets to them.
The families who went up send word back. The word is always the same word. Come up.
My father is teaching me to mend a roof that I do not think we will be living under.
I have said that out loud exactly once. We finished the roof in silence.
We planted this year's trees on the high ground instead of the garden. That is a decision, quietly made.
Somebody is writing a list of what has been abandoned here so that it is at least written somewhere.
There is talk of carrying the bell up the hill. Moving the bell would make it official.
I am going to be the last person my age here. I have done the arithmetic on that twice.
Sums in the morning, letters after. Every day. My hands are permanently chalky.
The terraces need weeding on both sides and there are nine of them and I am one person.
Everything up here has to be carried up, including the water, which I would like noted.
The goats are cleverer than anyone gives them credit for and it is genuinely a problem.
The wind takes the washing off the line every time and everybody is astonished every time.
There is a plum tree that only fruits on the leeward side. Everyone here can explain why, at length.
It is colder up here and people announce that as though it were information.
I copy pages until my hand cramps. Then I am given a different pen and told to keep going.
This village exists because the one below it went under. That is the entire reason for it.
They write down where the water reached each year, in a ledger, with the date beside it.
From the top field you can see the sea and it is closer than it is in the drawing on the wall.
Nobody up here builds below the third marker post. There is a rule and the rule has a number.
My family came up four generations back and we are still called the new ones.
The old road climbs up here and then stops at nothing, because the something is under water.
We can see the stilt village from here. They are on sticks. We are on rock. They think we are cowards.
The terraces are cut so the rain runs off without taking the soil. That was copied from somewhere else.
The ledger lists every house lost, the year it went, the family, and what they managed to save.
It does not say that one of them sang while she gutted fish, in a voice like a gull with a grievance.
Nobody was measuring the singing. That is the part that gets me about the ledger.
My great-grandmother carried plum stones up here in her mouth because both hands were full.
Four stones, two trees. She is under the smaller one and the smaller one is the one that fruits.
There are keys hanging by our door for houses that have been underwater since before my mother.
One whole shelf of the ledger is a single year. One year. One shelf.
We keep a chair that came up from the low house. Nobody sits in it. Nobody will move it either.
Our terraces copy the mountain place, where they built well and did not drown.
We copied a drawing of a drawing, my grandfather says, and he says it with real feeling.
The record keeper argues the carved city with anyone who sits down at his table.
Carved, not built, therefore older than the water, therefore the world had a before. That is his whole case.
He is right. He is also the reason people eat standing up in his house.
The pointy markers all stand on high ground, which people say proves the builders knew what high ground was.
The calendar stone is supposed to predict the water. My teacher says it predicts nothing at all.
She says that quietly, and only to us, and never when there are pilgrims in the village.
Everybody is copying books. Two of everything, then four. My hand cramps and I have complained formally.
The answer I got was: somebody has to be able to read this in fifty years. That shut me up.
We are writing the names of the drowned villages down before the last person who saw them dies.
There are four such people left. Four. That number is why everybody is in such a hurry.
They planted an entire orchard this spring that fruits in nine years. Somebody did that sum on purpose.
The seed jars go into the cave where it is cold. Not to eat. To keep.
There is already a plan for where the stilt families go when they come up. Nobody has shown them the plan.
Nobody has told the lowlanders that. It would be an insult and it is also a kindness.
My mother says our job is remembering. It is a strange thing to be handed as a job.
Thin air, thin soup, thin walls. That is the joke here and it is still the joke.
Ice on the bucket most mornings. We only properly wash on the warm days.
The path down takes two hours and the path up takes four and it is the same path.
We burn dung because nothing grows tall enough to burn at this height.
Bringing the animals in before dark is my job and dark is very early up here.
There is nothing to farm, so people keep records instead. That is an actual answer people give.
I sleep next to the dog for the warmth and my mother has decided not to know about it.
From up here you can see the whole coast and it is a different shape from the map in the hall.
Nobody up here worries about the level. That is the entire reason there are people up here.
If it reaches us, my father says, it has reached everybody, so it will not be our problem alone.
The traders tell us which villages went under this year. It is a short list and it is never empty.
There is a map nailed up in the hall with a lot of it now simply wrong.
Nobody redraws it. Somebody just pencils in the new edge every few years, over the old one.
We came up two lifetimes ago and everybody still calls my family the new ones.
The dead go into the rock because you cannot dig a grave in ground like this.
There is a niche in the wall with a comb, a fishing weight and a milk tooth in it.
Nothing labels them. Somebody put them there, and then that somebody died as well.
My grandmother came up from a fishing village and has not touched a boat in fifty years.
There is a boat up here. On a mountain. Somebody carried it up and nobody living knows why.
The oldest names in the record are all from one drowned place, all in the same handwriting.
We eat out of a bowl from a house nobody alive has been inside. It is a good bowl.
My grandfather still ties knots the coast way and has not seen the coast since before I was born.
We are as high as the mountain terrace place and half as clever. My grandfather's line, not mine.
Pilgrims come up wanting salt. Always salt. It is for the walk along the great wall.
They are looking for the break where the sea supposedly came through. They have looked for generations.
There is no break. My mother says that at home and never says it where a pilgrim can hear.
Somebody up here owns a drawing of the carved city and charges people to look at it.
It is a bad drawing. It is also the only one, so he is doing very well out of it.
The calendar stone is meant to say when the water stops. Every pilgrim reads it differently and goes home certain.
The tomb is the one thing they all agree on. Even the arguing ones go quiet about the tomb.
We take in whoever comes up. There is a room kept ready and it is rarely empty for long.
Nobody asks new arrivals what they left behind. That is not politeness, it is a rule.
The record book has run out of pages twice and they made more pages both times.
I am learning the old hand, the difficult one, so the earliest pages do not go silent.
They are copying everything into two sets and one set goes deep into the cave, in the dry.
We are planting trees at this height for the first time ever. Nobody knows if they will take.
The oldest man here wants to be carried down to see the sea once before he dies.
Nobody has said yes and nobody has said no, and he is not getting any lighter.
It is the same temperature in here all year. Outside changes constantly. In here does not.
Trimming the lamps is my job. The soot has built a black stripe along the roof of the passage.
The stripe is thickest at the height of a walking adult, which tells you how long people have walked it.
Water drips into a stone basin and fills it by morning, every morning, at the same rate.
The basin is worn into the rock. That is not carving. That is just the drip, taking its time.
The floor of the front chamber has been swept so long it now sits dished in the middle.
Nobody goes past the third lamp without telling somebody. That is the only real rule down here.
People have lived in here longer than anywhere else. Longer than the villages by a lot.
The old entrance is underwater now. Fish go in and out of it. We use the upper one.
Things come in here when the low villages give up on keeping them dry.
They moved the seed jars deeper in after a wet winter, because deeper is drier.
There is a water mark on the wall from a flood so old nobody knows which flood it was.
Everybody's grandparents' things end up in here eventually. Ours are on the fourth shelf along.
The stone does not change. People say that constantly, and they say it like it is a comfort.
It is not a comfort. It just means the stone is not the thing that is moving.
The dead lie in the fourth chamber with their feet towards the entrance. All of them, the same way.
The oldest lie deepest, so walking in is walking backwards through everybody.
There is a niche holding a comb, a fishing weight and a milk tooth, and no name anywhere near it.
Three people, or one person's whole life. Nobody can tell any more, and that is the point of it.
Read along the jar labels and the writing changes halfway down the shelf. Same shelf, two people, decades apart.
The first hand stopped. The second hand carried on. Nobody has ever explained that to me.
Books are stacked spine out in the dry chamber and the ones about the sea are read to pieces.
Somebody copied an entire book into the margins of another book, having run out of paper.
There are ochre handprints along the low passage at the height of a walking adult.
One line of them is smaller and lower and keeps stopping, which is a child keeping up.
Seven shapes are painted in a row on the deep wall: a triangle, a long line, a ring of arches, and four more.
Everyone agrees the triangle is the markers and the line is the great wall. After that it is a fight.
There is a charcoal drawing of the ring of arches with a water line ruled dead straight across it.
Under the line somebody has written a number. Nobody agrees what the number counts.
People bring their worst arguments down here. The echo does something to them and everybody leaves more certain than they came.
Carved, not built. Say it in the dark and it comes back sounding like proof, which is the trick.
A calendar of small squares is cut into the rock by the entrance and the squares run out four winters back.
Whoever was cutting them stopped. Nobody has picked it up. Everybody walks past it every day.
The seed jars are in two sets now. The back set is sealed with wax and is not for us.
I asked who the back set is for and got the longest silence of my life.
There is a new shelf down here, planed smooth and pegged in, completely empty, built to fit books.
Built to fit books that have not been written. Somebody measured a future and made a shelf for it.
The copying is done in here because it is dry. Two of everything, then four, then deeper in.
They are teaching me the way out in the dark, by hand, by count of turns. That is a lesson now.
